clue.text: Eccentric newspaper hack everyone follows about

indicators.note: 'follows' is a placement instruction rather than a description: the pieces named before it queue up behind the short word at the end of the clue.

parts.note: a book about birds is a book of birds, so the two words swap in this sense
the Financial Times, whose initials are crosswordland's favourite paper
to hack at a log is to hew it
everyone present is all of them

explanation.walkthrough: The surface hands you 'newspaper hack' as one job title, and the parse splits it into two unrelated pieces: a paper's initials and a verb about chopping wood.
explanation.definitionFit: Eccentric → OFF-THE-WALL: the idiom means wildly unconventional, as though bouncing away from any straight line, and it is everyday English rather than a crossword-only sense.

clue.text: Move supply of iron by crossing lake

indicators.note: 'crossing' means passing right through something, so the letter it introduces ends up inside the other piece instead of alongside it.

parts.note: the chemical symbol for the metal
three by four is written 3 x 4, so 'by' is the multiplication sign
the standard map abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is 'supply of iron', which reads as a delivery of metal. Split it the other way: 'supply' is an adverb, and the definition stops right there.
explanation.definitionFit: Move supply → FLEX: 'supply' is the adverb of 'supple', so the definition asks for movement that bends and gives, which is what flexing is.

clue.text: Fried tortilla drunk flipped with cry of accomplishment

indicators.note: 'flipped' means turned over the way you turn a pancake, so the three letters it governs are read from their far end back.

parts.note: a sot is a habitual soak, and here the word is a noun, not an instruction
ta-da is what you shout when you produce something with a flourish

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' sits next to a food word and looks exactly like an anagram signal. It is a noun instead, and the only thing done to it is a turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Fried tortilla → TOSTADA: in Mexican cooking a tostada is precisely that, a tortilla fried flat and crisp so that toppings can be piled on it.

clue.text: E.g. more time for homework available after turning sixteen

indicators.note: the word for available comes after the rearranged letters
turning means changing round, so the letters of the word sixteen are rearranged

parts.note: on means available, as in a dish being on the menu

explanation.surface: A sixteen-year-old pupil is given more time for homework.
explanation.definitionFit: An extension is an extra period allowed beyond a deadline, such as more days for coursework.

clue.text: A starry role, with moon involved?

definitions.text: A starry role, with moon involved?

indicators.note: 'involved' means tangled up with something, and letters tangled together do not come out in the order they went in.

parts.note: eleven letters taken straight off the front of the clue
four more letters joining the pile before it is shuffled

explanation.walkthrough: Every word does double duty here: read once it describes the job, read again it is fifteen letters and an instruction. That is what &lit means.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the post is a senior crown appointment in astronomy, so its holder's work genuinely is stars and moon, and the question mark flags the whimsy.

clue.text: Shade of flowering tree in India, during visit to north

indicators.note: 'during' means in the middle of a stretch, so the letter it introduces lands inside the other piece rather than beside it.
north is up the page, and this entry runs down it, so the letters travel against the grid and are read the other way round.

parts.note: a visit is a call — you pay someone a call
India is I in the NATO alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'India' is the misdirection. The country is not where the tree grows, and 'visit' is a noun rather than the verb the sentence wants.
explanation.definitionFit: Shade of flowering tree → LILAC: the pale mauve colour is named after the blossom of the shrub, so the plant's name doubles as the name of its own colour.

clue.text: Appear keen to serve venison one day?

definitions.meaning: the verb: a courtier or a dog at your feet, showing exaggerated eagerness to please
the noun: an animal defined by what it will grow into rather than by what it is now

explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are unrelated in origin, which is what makes the pairing land — a servile courtier and a young deer have nothing in common but four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses of one word: to fawn is to grovel for favour, and a fawn is a young deer — the meat it will become is the question mark's joke.

clue.text: Avoid terror gripping globe

indicators.note: 'gripping' is holding tight in a closed fist, so the piece doing the gripping shuts around whatever is named next.

parts.note: terror is fear at full strength
an orb is any sphere, and the globe is the sphere we live on

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gripping terror' is a phrase you have read a hundred times, which is exactly why the eye slides over it and misses that only one of those words is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Avoid → FORBEAR: to forbear is to hold back from an action, which is how you avoid something by choosing simply not to do it.

clue.text: Women given orders by nice young wizard

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation, as on a lavatory door
you are under whoever gives you your orders
a plain synonym in the sense of good-natured

explanation.walkthrough: 'Wizard' is not a robed spellcaster but the everyday sense, a wizard with numbers. The orders in the clue are the ones you take, not the ones you give.
explanation.definitionFit: young wizard → WUNDERKIND: German for 'wonder child', it names someone brilliant at a thing while still very young, with 'wizard' in its whiz-at-something sense.

clue.text: Watch dog, say, beginning to splash through wee in Paris

indicators.note: through here means passing inside the French word for wee

parts.note: petit is French for small, i.e. wee

indicators.note: only the first letter of splash is wanted

parts.note: its first letter S

explanation.surface: A dog's toilet stop described with some French thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wee' looks like the toilet sense, but it means small, and 'in Paris' asks for the French word.
explanation.definitionFit: To pet-sit is to look after someone's animal while they are away, and a dog is one example.

clue.text: Patient alert, not wandering

indicators.note: 'wandering' is straying off any fixed route, and letters that stray will not stay in the order they were given.

parts.note: eight letters lifted straight from the clue in the order the setter printed them

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a note on a hospital chart. 'Patient' is the definition and an adjective there, not a person in a bed, which is the whole misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Patient → TOLERANT: both describe someone who puts up with irritation without complaining, and the word is an adjective in each case, not a noun.

clue.text: Spooner's family all named after original matriarch, a queen

indicators.note: Dr Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the sounds of the phrase get exchanged

parts.note: a clan is a family group
of Eves: everyone named after Eve, the first mother; EEVZ is how Eves is said

explanation.surface: A family history in which every woman is named after the first ancestor.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is 'clan of Eves'; 'Spooner's' swaps its opening sounds, the CL of clan moving to Eves, so 'an of Cleves' is heard: 'Anne of Cleves'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne of Cleves was the fourth wife of Henry VIII and so briefly Queen of England.

clue.text: Gaunt head of operations keeping rogue state and America apart

indicators.note: keeping means holding something in, so the letter goes inside the other pieces
apart says the letter keeps two of the pieces separated by sitting between them

parts.note: a cad is a rogue, a dishonourable man
to aver is to state firmly
US, the United States

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A haggard operations chief keeps a rogue nation and the USA from each other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rogue state' reads as one idea, but rogue and state are separate pieces, and the operations letter sits between the last two.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadaverous means corpse-like, extremely thin and pale, which is what a gaunt face looks like.

clue.text: Hunting trip mostly free of risk and very dry

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so each word loses its last letter

parts.note: safe means free of risk
arid means very dry, and the same 'mostly' trims it to its first three letters

explanation.surface: A description of a hunting trip that is mostly safe in a dry climate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' does double duty: it trims SAFE to SAF and ARID to ARI.
explanation.definitionFit: A safari is an expedition in Africa, traditionally to hunt or observe wild animals.

clue.text: Facing out

definitions.meaning: the cricket sense: of the two batters at the wicket, the one the bowler is aiming at
the industrial sense: a workforce that has stopped work is said to be out

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two definitions, no wordplay at all. Short clues like this are often the hardest, because there is nothing to take apart and no indicator to find.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the batter receiving the bowling is on strike, so is facing; workers who have downed tools and walked out are on strike too.

clue.text: Plan huge upset after kick-off, moving right up

indicators.note: the overturned word comes after the altered start
in a down answer, moving the right letter up means it climbs one place earlier

parts.note: a kick-off is the start of a match

indicators.note: in a down answer, upset means turned upside down, so read from the bottom

parts.note: mega means huge

explanation.surface: A plan for a huge upset after kick-off, with a right-sided player pushed up the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: In START, R moves one place up to give STRAT; MEGA turned upside down is AGEM.
explanation.definitionFit: A stratagem is a scheme or trick for gaining an advantage, a cunning plan.

clue.text: Mathematician telephoned Euler's number after delay

indicators.note: 'after' is a positional instruction: the two pieces named before it sit behind the one word named at the end.

parts.note: a lag is a delay between two things
to telephone somebody is to ring them
e is the constant behind natural logarithms, about 2.718

explanation.walkthrough: A whole mathematical constant standing in for a single letter is a trick worth banking — 'Euler's number' looks like a fact to know and is really one character.
explanation.definitionFit: Mathematician → LAGRANGE: definition by example, Joseph-Louis Lagrange being an eighteenth-century giant of mechanics and number theory.

clue.text: Turn money into Euro abroad

indicators.note: the money goes inside the rearranged letters
abroad suggests being scattered widely, so the letters of Euro are rearranged

parts.note: tin is slang for money

explanation.surface: Advice to exchange your cash into euros when travelling abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' reads as a verb in the surface but is the noun, a stage act; tin is old slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: A routine is a set act or performance, as a comedian's turn on stage.

clue.text: Stormy piece by Joplin with one sharp?

parts.note: Scott Joplin wrote ragtime, and one ragtime composition is a rag
a key signature of a single sharp is G major, so such a piece is written in G

explanation.walkthrough: 'Joplin' wants to be Janis and is Scott. The question mark then flags the key signature as a roundabout way of naming one particular note.
explanation.definitionFit: Stormy → RAGING: a raging storm is the stock phrase, and on its own the word describes weather at its most violent pitch.

clue.text: Hateful gin has one turning to rum in the morning

indicators.note: the one changes into the new letters, so I is swapped out

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one
rum means odd, strange
AM, ante meridiem, before noon

explanation.surface: A drinker's grumble about gin giving way to rum at breakfast time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink beside gin, but it means odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Goddamn is an intensifying curse word, so something goddamn is cursed or hateful.

clue.text: Hunt traitor with likely winner outside kept apart

indicators.note: 'outside' puts one piece around the others, which means its own letters split so that some lead and the rest follow.

parts.note: a seed in tennis is a ranked player expected to go far in the draw
as a noun, a hunt for something is a quest
to rat on someone is to betray them, so a rat is the betrayer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunt' opens the clue with a capital letter and a verb's shape, which is the misdirection: it is a noun, and it is not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: kept apart → SEQUESTRATED: to sequestrate is to seize property and hold it aside, so what has been sequestrated is shut away from whoever owned it.

clue.text: Incredibly, cap's all made of the same material

definitions.text: all made of the same material

parts.note: 'incredibly hot' just means 'hot' with an intensifier, and this is the shortest one
the cap on a jar is its lid

explanation.walkthrough: 'Incredibly' at the head of a clue, with a comma after it, looks like an anagram signal. Here it is plain fodder: a two-letter synonym is all it hands over.
explanation.definitionFit: all made of the same material → SOLID: solid gold means gold right through rather than plated, so this is the uniform-substance sense, not the hard-not-soft one.

clue.text: Attend course for police

parts.note: to attend a thing is to be present at it, and this is the verb that phrase opens with
the second half of that same two-word phrase — you attend something by being at it

explanation.walkthrough: A four-letter answer with only three words of clue: 'Attend' is not a definition at all but a single word that unpacks into a two-word phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: course for police → BEAT: a constable's beat is the fixed round they walk, so the ground itself takes its name from the pacing that covers it.

clue.text: Royal Marine crosses Roman road in high spirits

indicators.note: 'crosses' means goes over the top of, so one piece lies across the other and has to open up to let it through.

parts.note: a jolly is old naval slang for a Royal Marine
via is simply Latin for road, and 'Roman' tells you which language to use

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are vocabulary rather than mechanism, which is why this one is either instant or impossible: you either know the naval slang or you do not.
explanation.definitionFit: in high spirits → JOVIALLY: jovial comes from Jove, whose planet was held to make people merry, so to act jovially is to act cheerfully.

clue.text: Was an idler after golf given coat then fired?

indicators.note: 'after' is positional: what it introduces goes in front, so the single letter ends up leading and the longer word trails it.

parts.note: G in the NATO alphabet, the same table that gives India and Whiskey
the past tense is doing real work — it is what makes the tense of the answer come out right

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the warning label: 'fired' here means a kiln rather than a dismissal, and 'coat' is a layer of liquid rather than something you wear.
explanation.definitionFit: given coat then fired? → GLAZED: pottery is glazed by brushing on a coat of glaze and baking it in a kiln, which is both halves at once.

clue.text: In centre of Paris, level area for Notre-Dame?

indicators.note: 'In centre of' points at where letters sit rather than at what words mean, and the middle of the stretch that follows is where to look.

parts.note: four letters in a row, straddling both the comma and the space between the two words

explanation.walkthrough: Punctuation is the disguise. A concealed answer that runs across a comma is far harder to see than one buried inside a single long word.
explanation.definitionFit: area for Notre-Dame? → ISLE: the cathedral was built on an island in the Seine, so the question mark flags one particular one standing for the class.

clue.text: Peel apart, eat lime and bananas

indicators.note: 'bananas' means driven out of your mind, and letters sent out of their minds will not keep the places they were in.

parts.note: ten letters taken straight from the clue, in the order they are printed

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a fruit bowl and 'Peel' plays along with it. It is the definition, and a verb — the fruit is only there to be shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Peel apart → DELAMINATE: a laminate is built from bonded layers, so to delaminate is for those layers to come unstuck and lift away from each other.
